column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The entry says Husayn ibn Ali seized power during an invasion from Algiers; the article does not mention this, so it is not repeated or contradicted. The current head of the family (born 1929) is left out as a present-day detail.

The article gives the day of the attack inconsistently: its lead says Ali was struck on 28 January 661 and died two days later, its later section that he was struck on 26 January and died on 28 January. No day is given in the text.
The article dates Toikka's Birds both to 1962 (lead) and 1971 (design history), so no year is given. The Aalto vase of 1936, already in the entry, is not repeated.

The article dates the party's formation to 1874 under Isaac Butt and its dissolution to 1918, while the entry's dates are 1882–1922. The text tells the 1874 group as a forerunner and gives neither a founding year nor a year of dissolution.

The article gives his birth as c. 1438/1439 or c. 1440 (and age 16 in 1456), and his reign as from 1460 or 1464; the entry gives c. 1438 and rule from 1463. No birth year, age or reign start is given. The article does not mention the taking of Famagusta from the Genoese.

The article gives the dead of the 1971 uprising both as nearly 5,000 and as an estimated 30,000 insurgents according to the JVP; neither figure is given. The article's laudatory passage on Dissanayake's leadership is not used, and nothing is said about the present government.

The article gives his birth as c. 1720 by one source and more likely in the 1730s by Thomas Philipp; the entry has c. 1720. It dates his governorship of Sidon to 1776 (and in one place 1777), the entry to 1775. Neither the birth year nor the start of the governorship is given.
The article dates the court's last stand west of the Seta Bridge to 22 August in one section and the battle at Seta and Ōtomo's death to 20 and 21 August in its list of events; no day is given.
The article says only that he entered France with four thousand troops in 1576; the entry's 1575–1576 campaign is not dated in the text.

The article gives the number of copies of the Massachusett Bible inconsistently (more than two thousand, 1,180 volumes by 1663, 1,000 copies) and dates the translation to 1660 as well as its printing to 1663; no count is given. It does not date Natick's founding.
The article does not say how his first marriage ended.

The entry dates his sweeter strain to around 1612; the article has commercial cultivation from 1611 and export from 1612, which does not contradict it. The article does not mention the peace that followed the marriage, already in the entry.

The entry says Gamarra was killed at Ingavi; the article says Ballivián took him prisoner and ordered him executed. How Gamarra died is not stated. The article's ages (18 when he joined Lanza, 37 at Ingavi) do not fit a birth in 1805 and are left out.

The article names his wife both as Ana and as Brianda (Reyna) Mendes, Gracia's daughter; the text says only that he married his cousin, a daughter of Gracia Mendes Nasi. Its sentence that he 'escaped to Portugal' after Charles I decided to confiscate the Mendes fortune is unclear and left out.

The article dates Kaabu 1537-1867; the entry says it emerged in the 13th century as a province of Mali and later became independent. I gave no founding year for the federation. Left out the article's claim that Kaabu's wars produced up to half of the Africans sold into slavery in the 17th and 18th centuries: the scope (Senegambia or all Africa) is unclear.

The entry says the fort was a Chandela stronghold until Aibak took it in 1203; the article says Trailokyavarman retook it within a couple of years and later Chandelas held it to at least 1289. Left the later Chandela period out. The entry has the fort pass to the British in 1812; the article gives East India Company management in 1805-06, annexation in 1812, a British garrison in 1857 and a capture on 4 May 1858, partly contradicting itself. Left the colonial period out. The article gives the height as 367 m (lead) and 408 m (geography) above sea level; used only the 244 m above the plain, which both agree on.

Atreyi Biswas holds that the first Karkota ruler was Durlabhaka Pratapaditya, with his father Durlabhavardhana a subordinate of the Huna king Narendraditya Khinkhila; the entry names Durlabhavardhana as founder, so I did not give her alternative founder.
The entry says Keban created 'one of Turkey's largest reservoirs'; the article calls it reputedly the fourth-largest lake. I gave no rank.
The entry says the missionaries took relics to Goa; the article says some were taken to Georgia (Alaverdi) and the rest were said to have been buried in Goa. Worded to fit both.
The entry's ritual role at the court of Luang Prabang is not in the article; not touched.
The article says the Spanish entered in the 15th century; left the century out.

The entry dates the culture to the early 3rd millennium BCE; the article gives c. 3300-2800 BCE, 3300-2600 BCE and an earliest layer of 2605 BC. Left all dates of the culture out. Left out the Rani Kot section, which concerns another fort (Ranikot). The article gives the Pakistan Department of Archaeology excavations as 1955 and 1957 and F. A. Khan's as 1954-55; used only the latter.
The excerpt names Ljotić only by surname; no first name given.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the description
The article says members of kuge families remain influential in Japanese society today; left out as a present-day claim.

The article dates the Vienna manuscript to the '8th century', an evident slip; no date given. The comparison with song contests is inferred from the article's list of influences; the article lists them under Influences without saying in what respect.
The entry's mention of Centurione II Zaccaria dying there in 1432 is not in the article; not repeated.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little beyond the description
The article says women were not allowed in the Appenzell Innerrhoden Landsgemeinde 'up to 1991'; phrased as first admitted in 1991.

The entry says Byzantine and Lazic forces retook Petra in 551 and held most of the country; the article gives no year for Bessas's capture of Petra and says the Persians went on to seize 'the lion's share of Lazica'. Gave neither the year nor that judgement. The article names 'Dr. Richard Fyre' (sic) and 'The Persian Empire encyclopedia'; left the names out rather than correct them from memory.

The article's account of the 1960 election (women disfranchised) is garbled; only the fourth place is used. The article dates his premiership 1965-1986; the entry speaks of leading the party from independence in 1966, which does not contradict this.
The article calls him 'Leodegar of Poitiers'. Its sequence of exile and death is compressed; the year of execution is left to the entry (679).

The entry calls it the longest poem of pre-imperial China; the article says only 'one of the longest', so neither is repeated. The article dates the poem to the 3rd century BCE; the entry places Qu Yuan in the late 4th century BCE, so no century is given for the poem here beyond the 299 BCE limit.

The article reports Bruneian claims to Limbang in 1951, 1963 and 1973 and the 2009 maritime agreement, with Brunei denying it had dropped the claim; the entry's 'largely settled in 2009' is left as it stands and not repeated. The article's date of annexation is 17 March 1890; the entry gives 1890, consistent.
The article calls Owain Whitetooth (Owain Danwyn) king of Gwynedd; kept as given.
The article does not date the founding of Fort Frontenac; the entry's 1673 is left to the entry. The article's spelling varies between Duchesnau and Duchesneau; Duchesneau used.

The entry says his brother Henry Raspe succeeded him; the article says he was succeeded by his five-year-old son Hermann II under the tutelage of Henry Raspe. The succession is left out. The entry says he died at Otranto; the article says he died before reaching Otranto, so the place of death is not named.
Article title is 'Louis Rudolph, Duke of Brunswick'. The entry's 'younger son' and the article's 'youngest son' agree.
The article does not mention the Church of Our Lady, the imperial ban or Burghausen; those stay in the entry only.

The article does not date his break with Santa Cruz (1838 in the entry). It says Salaverry overthrew him in 1835 and that he then 'executed' Salaverry. Death date 5 February 1847 in the article; the year only is used.
The excerpt's section on Dharmakṣema's northern edition is empty; the Northern Liang is not mentioned in the file and is left to the entry.
The article's opening says the family ruled Rimini until 1500; its later text gives 1528 for the city's final incorporation into the Papal States, matching the entry's dates.

The article's lead speaks of a Rajasuya sacrifice performed by Pushyamitra; its plot summary and the entry speak of his sacrificial horse, so the Rajasuya is left out. Its plot summary several times calls the king 'Mayank', apparently a slip; Agnimitra is used. The article says simply that it is his first play; the entry says probably the earliest, so the point is not restated.

The article credits him with building the Janjira Fort in 1567, when he was nineteen and still a slave by its own account; left out as doubtful. The article's account of his death in a duel with a Dadhiwadiya Charan of Marwar is unclear and left out. It gives the Aurangabad renaming both as 'the 1650s' and as 1653.

The entry's wording ('Lucius Licinius Lucullus, who was consul in 73 BCE') can be read as giving the consulship to Lucius; the article gives it to Marcus. The year of the consulship is therefore left out of this text. The entry lists Odessos and Mesembria among the cities taken; the article lists Apollonia, Kallatis, Tomi and Istros, so no list of cities is given. The entry dates his death c. 56 BCE, the article 'soon after 56 BC'.
The article gives the reign as 855-819 BC without 'c.'; the entry's circa dates are not restated. The throne base relief from Nimrud is in the entry; the article describes it without naming Nimrud.
The article says the date and circumstances of her death are uncertain; the entry's 'd. 1503' is not repeated.

The article does not date the handover of Tyrol to the Habsburgs; the entry's 1363 is left to the entry. The article calls her second husband Louis I of Brandenburg (a Wittelsbach); the entry calls him Louis of Bavaria. No contradiction, but the entry's form is not repeated. The Charles IV siege is dated 'the next year' after 1346, i.e. 1347.
SKIPPED: The article is a list of margraves and electors whose tables are not in the saved text; its prose is under 250 words and adds little to the description.

The article gives her birth as c. 1545; the entry has c. 1544, so no birth year is given. The article does not mention the alliance with Kabarda or her brother Mikhail Cherkassky; those stay in the entry.

The article has him flee first to Chile and stay some months in Santiago before going to Lima; the entry says he fled to Peru. The Chilean stay is left out. The legends of the white horse and the marching guard are left out as anecdote.

The article's lead calls Ottone his uncle and dates his appointment as Captain of the People to 1287; the body calls Ottone his great-uncle and links the appointment to the battle of Desio of 1277. The entry says great-nephew, so great-uncle is used and no year given. The order of the 1311 events and of the heresy case (December) is muddled in the article; only the clear dates are used.
The article gives no years for the Italian invasion or the German occupation; none are given here.

SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance: a list of rebellions, a kidnapping and present-day fighting, nothing on the town's history before 1916 (the entry's Kel Ataram and French post are not in it)
The article says his son was sold into slavery in the West Indies in one place and his wife and son in Bermuda in another; no place is given here.

The article dates his state funeral to 30 April 1940, which seems a slip for a death on 27 March; the funeral date is left out. The iconic portrait is dated 1935 in one place and its publication 1936 in another; left out.
The article dates his accession as knez to 1046 and speaks of a rule of 30 or so years; the entry says he ruled from about 1050. The start year is left out.
The article dates the start of the uprising to 1914; the entry says he led it from 1915. No start year is given here.

The article says most researchers place his birth in 1717, while Salman Mumtaz gave 1733 and Firudin bey Kocharli named Hasansu as his birthplace; the entry dates him c. 1717, so no birth year or rival view is given here.
The article dates the helot revolt to 465 BC; the entry dates the earthquake to about 464 BCE. No year is given here.
The article gives too little for a third section (nothing on his early life or on the succession after him).
The article's paragraph on his sons' migration to Pakistan is incoherent and left out.

The article's section on uncertainties cites Portuguese letters of 1513 and Tomé Pires to argue that his conversion took place in 1514-1515, which contradicts his death c. 1402 and the entry's 1368; the argument is left out. His reign is given as from 1363/68; no start year is used.
The article says he first fled to the Republic of the Congo and later moved to Switzerland; the entry says he left for Europe in 1965. The Congo stage is left out.
The chronicle says he was captured; a contemporary letter says he and his son were killed. Both given, attributed.

The entry calls Prapanca a court poet; the article says he wrote incognito after retiring from the court. Worded as the article has it without denying he had been at court. UNESCO: regional register 2008, 'finally registered it in 2013' (unclear which register); gave only 2008.
The article gives the 1932 census majority of 51% once as Christian and once as Maronite Christian; used 'Christian'.
Article: 'Early evidence of salt extraction dates back to the end of the first millennium BC' and also ceramics of the 4th century BC showing salt extraction; used the ceramics only.
The article says the Alhambra Decree required both Jews and Muslims to convert or leave Spain and Portugal; left out as confused.
The article names her only as Shipley; her first name is left out.
SKIPPED: article has about 200 words of substance beyond a list of works, and gives his death as 1272 against the entry's c. 1269

Excavation start: the article says 10 February 1942; the entry says excavations since 1944. Date left out. Period: the article has Funan and the port from the 2nd century BC to the 12th century AD; the entry dates the site 1st-7th century. Span left out.

The article gives his birth as c. 985 in the lead and around 983 in the text; not given. It dates the seizure of Champagne after Stephen I's death in 1019/1020, while its lead and the entry give 1022; the year is left out.
Zhmud is named only by surname in the source.
Samnite wars given in the article as 370 BC to 290 BC, which looks like a slip; left out.

The entry calls Landry Otto-William's son-in-law; the article first calls Landric his stepson, then lists Matilda as Landri's wife. I name Landri without a relationship when telling of Nevers, and give Matilda's marriage as the article lists it. Reginald I, Count of Burgundy, his son, left out for length.

SKIPPED: The article covers only the present-day municipality: a list of localities, land use and economy; nothing of the obsidian workshops, the Aztec craft centre or the battle of 1520 that the entry tells.

The entry says he was among the first Welsh rulers styled prince of the Welsh; the article says he was the first recorded to do so. I give the titles without saying first. The article gives his death as 23 November 1170 in the lead.
The article does not mention the Battle of Talas that the entry names; I neither repeat nor contradict it.
The popular-culture section (a 2026 video game) left out. The entry's 'parting shot' is not in the article; not repeated.

The entry dates the storming of Ganja to January 1804; the article says early 1804. I give the year only. The article's lead names the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 among his wars; its body gives that of 1787–92 with battles. I give only the latter. The entry names Huseyngulu Khan; the article does not name the khan of Baku.
The article speaks of the 'capture of Illyria'; the entry says Philip kept 'most of his gains in Illyria'. I wrote 'its gains in Illyria'. The article does not mention the Epirotes' mediation.

The entry says he executed most of Fort Caroline's men; the article says all adult men encountered were killed (132) while Laudonnière and several score escaped. I give the article's figure. The article tells the Calusa contact after his 1567 return and appointment to Cuba; the order of his later travels is unclear, so I give them without dates.

The article names his first wife both Micaela Antonia Rivera de Soto and Micaela Antonia del Rivero; I leave the name out. The article's lead says he is today considered a dictator; I attribute the judgement to the historians the article names instead.
Present seat counts in the House and local divisions left out (time-bound). The article does not mention the labour unrest of 1938.

The article says Charles VIII was soon crowned, 'ending the need for a regency government', while the entry says the couple governed during his minority from 1483. I avoid saying when the regency ended. The article reports contradictory accounts of a son, Charles, born in 1476; left out.

The article says the Russian appanage of 1795 helped him buy the Berlin palace in 1782; I give the purchases without linking them to the appanage. The entry's 'quarrelled constantly with the Courland nobility' is not in the article; not repeated.
The article calls him the country's last uparaja; left out as a ranking-like claim it does not explain.

The article's lead gives his death as 6 January 1786 (as the entry's dates) but its body says he died at Lyon in 1772; I leave the year out of the text. The entry says intendant 1767–1772; the article's lead says 1766–1772 but the body says the post was offered in 1766 and he sailed in 1767. I give the offer in 1766 and the sailing in 1767. The article says he raided Cebu, Mindanao and Borneo as 'Dutch territories'; I wrote 'Dutch-held islands' generally.
The article dates his rule 340–334 BC ('six years') and his death before the landing of 334; the entry has c. 340–335 and death c. 335. I give no years for his rule or death.

The article says he died before the gates of Rajagaha after fleeing; it does not say he was seeking Ajatashatru's help, as the entry does. Not contradicted. Short article: the text uses nearly all of it.
The entry says she 'negotiated vassalage with Bayezid I'; the article says she accepted Ottoman suzerainty in summer 1390. Consistent.

The entry dates independence to around 163 BCE and says he ruled as an independent king. The article gives the conventional date 163/162 BC but says some recent scholars prefer 150 BC on coin evidence, and that he probably never styled himself king (the one 'basileus' at Gerger being a later honour from Antiochus I). I leave both the date of independence and the royal title out of the text.

The entry dates his reign c. 610–642; the article gives r. 609–642 and says the year of accession is debated (c. 610–611). I give no accession year. The entry says he was killed when Narasimhavarman I captured Badami in 642; the article says he was defeated and possibly killed in c. 642–643. I leave his end out of the text.
The entry dates the defeat of Axayacatl to 1479; the article says only the 1470s, so the year is left to the entry. The friar's name is spelt Acalá as in the article (usually Alcalá).

Dates of the town's life differ: the entry has about the 1st century BCE to the 5th century CE; the article has it emerging in the 4th century BC, flourishing from the 3rd century BC to the 3rd century AD, and abandoned by the Kinda around 300 AD. The span is left out. The article gives the King Saud University excavations as 1972-1995 in one sentence and 1970-2003 in the next; the entry says from 1972. Excavation dates left out. The 'Current Condition' section (visitor centre never built, 'to date') was not used as it is written as if still current.

Birth year differs within the article (c. 1845 in the lead, about 1850 in his own letter, 1852 on his tombstone); no birth year given here. The article says the Pease River account of his presence is disputed, so his escape is left out.

The article's lead says the Rada moved from Minsk to Grodno; its Formation section gives Vilnius, Hrodna, then Kaunas. The fuller sequence is used. The article dates the founding of the Congress's council to 31 December 1918, an evident slip (it preceded March 1918); no date given. Left out: the article's characterisation of Lukashenko's policies, and 'as of' statements on the Rada's present role.
SKIPPED: too little material: the article has about 150 words of history (the 1114 inscription, the 1407 division, Bimbaji Bhonsle, British rule) and otherwise census figures and transport
The article is short (about 500 words); two sections only. The return of the relics in 1989 (in the entry) is not in the article and is not repeated.
Jordanes's version that Rechiar took ship in the Tyrrhenian Sea is left out; the article calls it almost certainly wrong.
The article describes the party as 'white supremacist'; the entry calls it 'white conservative'. Neither label repeated; the policies are described.
The entry's capture by Owain Gwynedd in 1167 is not in the article and is not repeated. Short article: about 300 words written.
The entry dates the wage and price freeze from 1982; the article's section on it is cut in this copy, so no year is given here.
The entry's 'substantially larger Sasanian force' is not in the article and not repeated.
The article lists more than twenty laws repealed with it in March 1922, including the Police Act 1861 and Section 144 CrPC, which looks doubtful; only the act's own repeal is given.
The article's lead says the line ran along the Appalachians; its body speaks of the crest of the Allegheny Mountains and the Appalachian watershed. 'Appalachian watershed' used.

Entry's dates 1839-1895 kept; the article treats the expansion as beginning in the 16th century. Not stated in the text. The article's casualty figures for 1866 contain an evident slip ('more than 2,500 thousand killed' at Khujand); left out.

The article contradicts itself on the Hoysaleswara temple (built by Vishnuvardhana; built by Ketamalla in 1150; land granted 1121; consecrated around 1121) and on the Keshava temple (completed 1258 by 'King Somnath'; consecrated 1268 by Somanatha Dandanayaka). Their dates are left out.

The article says the order was founded by the mystic Zahed Gilani and named after his son-in-law and successor Safi al-Din, and calls it Kurdish; the entry says Safi al-Din founded it. The founding is left out of the text. Short article: two sections, about 290 words.

The entry calls her founder of Hohenburg; the article says her father founded the community for her. Who founded it is left out. The article dates the Life to the 9th century in one place and about the 10th century (based on an 8th-century Life) in another; written as 'her medieval Life'.

The article gives his death as 17 June 811 and also as the 3rd month of Kōnin 2, and a posthumous rank dated 27 May 811; only the year is given. Aterui, Isawa Castle and the appointment year 797 (in the entry) are not in the article and not repeated.

The entry places the lake about 80 km west of Jaipur; the article says 80 km south-west in its lead and 60 km south-west under Geography. No distance given. The article gives the 2019 bird deaths as more than 15,000 in one section and 18,000-23,000 in another; written as 'thousands'.
The article dates the Qing dynasty 1644-1910 (usually 1912); no dates given for it.

The article says the school was expelled from the Canal Zone in 1984 and its commandant oversaw the transfer to Fort Benning in 1984-1985; the entry's 1984 move stands and is not repeated. Ruth Blakeley's 2013 finding of greater transparency after 2001 left out for length.

The article says Scupi was 'included in Moesia Superior after the province was formed in AD 6'; the year left out as the province's date is uncertain in other sources. The theatre is also called 'the ancient Macedonian theater' and the restoration project an 'amphitheatre' with 9,000 seats: inconsistent, so the project's target not named. The Justiniana Prima link is hedged as the article presents it as an assumption.
The article says the movement ended with defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War 'in 1895'; the entry gives the war as 1894-1895, so the end is not restated.
The article gives his death as 29 November 997; the entry's dates give only 997, which agrees. The Gukjagam (992) in the entry is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article gives Wednesday and 4 December as his consecrated days in Candomblé, and the fifth day of the week in Yorubaland; both kept in their own contexts.

Eggeling dated the final written version to 300 BCE, with older oral elements; the entry says composed in the first half of the 1st millennium BCE, so Eggeling's date is left out to avoid an apparent contradiction.

The entry says the rising was suppressed by a 'state-funded militia'; the article says Lincoln's army was privately funded by merchants (later reimbursed by the state), alongside Shepard's state militia. Lincoln's merchant funding is told without calling it state- or privately funded. The article also says recent scholarship suggests Shays's role was exaggerated and that he denied being a leader; the entry calls him the leader, so this is left out.

The article gives his birth as 1072/1078 and 'the 1070s'; the entry's c. 1072 agrees with the first. The entry says he settled in Hakkari before 1111; the article gives only 'around the age of thirty', which is used. Bar Hebraeus calls him the one whom the Kurds of Mosul hold a prophet: left out for length.
Several later claims in the article (founder of world bureaucracy, first political scientist) are hedged there with 'perhaps' and left out.
The historian Shiramine Jun's explanation of the clan's inactivity (a power struggle between Yoshihisa and Ijūin Tadamune) left out for length.

The entry dates the seizure of Chūzan to 1406 and the conquests of Hokuzan to 1416 and Nanzan to 1429. The article puts the eunuch incident in 1406, Shishō's request for recognition in 1407, and says the official histories differ on the order and details of the conquests; it gives 1422 for a governor installed in Sanhoku and 1430 for Hashi as sole Ming tributary. No date is given for the coup or the conquests in the text. The traditional credit for agriculture and iron tools is unsupported by contemporary evidence, per the article; left out.

The article dates his time as Nawab from 5 October 1754 but also says he was recognised as Nawab after his father's death in 1753: no accession date given. Its territorial terms of the Treaty of Allahabad (Kora and Allahabad to the Company, 5 million rupees) and later cessions of Chunar, Benares, Ghazipur and Allahabad sit uneasily with the entry's 'kept his lands', so only the trade and alliance terms are told.
The article does not date the building of the Sihlsee or the Etzelwerk, so no date is given. Nothing on the Battle of St. Jakob an der Sihl in the article.
SKIPPED: the article has under 250 words of substance, most of it already in the entry (parents, tomb, excavators, jewellery and museums)
Legacy section is short; the abolition is the only end matter the article gives. The entry has 'around 1429'; the article gives 1429 without hedge, so no year is restated.
The Rajagopuram's claim to be the tallest in Asia is given 'as of 2016' and left out.
The entry calls it the most northerly cathedral in Britain; the article says the most northerly in the United Kingdom and the oldest in Scotland: not restated.
The article's lead dates the church 'from 1688' while its history section says it was built from 1668 to 1693; only the completion in 1693, common to both, is given.
The article does not mention the Nemesis, the Opium War or Perry, which the entry's description covers; nothing here touches them.
The article does not say where he died; the entry's 'in captivity in Luoyang' is not repeated or contradicted.
The article dates his reign 1002-1050 and his claim to the throne to 1010; the entry says about 1006-1050. Neither start year is given in the text.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words, mostly a list of members; too little to add 260 words

The article says the building was complete by 1958; the entry says it was completed only in the 1980s. No completion date is given in the text. The article says Sultan Jahan Begum continued the building after her mother's death in 1901 until the end of her own life; the entry says work stopped after 1901. The daughter's role is left out. Left out the 2014 world ranking and 'largest mosque in India' (ranking).
The article does not mention the crossing of the Kanmon Straits or the attack on Kokura in 1866 (entry); not repeated.
The article has almost no narrative history; the History section lists the historic sites it names.

The article calls Tansen the capital of the Magar Kingdom (Barha Magarat) and says local Magar kings lost influence in the 18th century; the entry calls it the capital of the Sen kings of Palpa until the Gorkha annexation of 1806. The text names neither the kingdom's character nor the date of its end. The article places Tansen in central Nepal; the entry says western Nepal. No region is given in the text.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words, most of it already in the entry

SKIPPED: the article is about the modern town of Tell Rifaat and its civil-war history; its material on the ancient site (Arpad) is about 150 words and dates the Assyrian capture to 743 BCE, against the entry's 740 BCE
The article says Spain transferred Louisiana to France in October 1802; the entry says Spain kept administering the colony until 1803. The date of the transfer is left out.
The article dates the excavation to 1978 (entry 1978-1979) and counts about 20,600 objects, later 22,000 (entry some 20,000); neither year nor count is given.

The article gives her death as 15 October 958 (and in 958 at the end) but also has her in royal charters in 959; the entry dates her 'after 958'. No death date is given in the text. The article calls her 'an aunt or cousin' of Abd al-Rahman III in one place and his aunt (her nephew) in another; the text follows 'nephew', as the entry says aunt.
The article says Tokharistan came under the First Turkic Khaganate by the 6th century; the entry has Turkic yabghus from the 7th century. No date is given for the start of Turkic rule.

The article gives his birth as around 1468 (entry c. 1465) and the departure for Canton as 1516 (entry 1517); neither year is given. The article says he was executed in 1524, or died of disease in 1524, or lived on to 1540 in Jiangsu without leave to depart; the entry dates his death c. 1540. The text says only that accounts differ.
The article says the TFG was established in Nairobi; the entry says formed at peace talks in Kenya: consistent.

Date conflict: the entry dates the treaty 24 September 1706, the article 13 October 1706. Neither date is printed in the longer text. The article does not mention the Swedish army wintering in Saxony (in the entry); not repeated.
The article contradicts itself on the ratification at Northampton: 1 May in the lead, 3 May in the Negotiations section. The entry says May; no day printed.
